title: Tree walks
description:
The starter defines a binary tree node that owns its children. Write:

```cpp
int height(const Node* root);                                    // -1 for an empty tree
bool sameTree(const Node* a, const Node* b);                     // same shape and values
std::vector<int> postorder(const Node* root);                    // WITHOUT recursion: use your own stack
std::vector<std::vector<int>> levels(const Node* root);          // values grouped by depth, left to right
std::unique_ptr<Node> build(const std::vector<int>& pre, const std::vector<int>& in);   // values are distinct
std::string serialize(const Node* root);                         // pre-order, "#" for an empty child, single spaces
std::unique_ptr<Node> deserialize(const std::string& text);
```

- `postorder` must not call itself: the tests give it a tree 100,000 levels deep.
- `build` gets the pre-order and in-order traversals of a tree and rebuilds it. Use a hash map from value to in-order position so that it is O(n): the tests rebuild a tree of 65,535 nodes.
- `serialize` of the tree with root 2, left child 1 and no right child is `"2 1 # # #"`; the empty tree is `"#"`.
hints: An easy iterative post-order: do a pre-order that pushes the left child **before** the right (so it visits node, right, left), then reverse the result to get left, right, node.
In `build`, keep an index into the pre-order that advances every time you create a node; the root of each range is the next pre-order value, and its in-order position splits the range.
